These impulses are of the "dry pulse" type which means that pulses cannot be applied (by the customer) to the utility's metering stations to disturb the metering system.
During the past two years, Duke Power Company has been using a 100 percent, 12-month ratchet for billing demand on large customers (commercial and industrial). This means that the customer's billing demand for the next 12-month billing period is 100 percent of the peak demand occurring during the previous 11 months.
The Duke Power Company has signed a contract with National Economic Research Associates, Inc. (NERA) to study long and short-term marginal cost economics as well as peakload and time-of-day metering as a means of reducing Applicant's peak loads and passing the marginal costs of peak demands to those customers who cause such peaks. NERA will recommend changes in rate schedules and metering procedures if the study indicates a need for such changes. This study will also provide the Applicant with estimates of the effects of possible rate schedule changes and time-of-day metering on system load factors and generating capacity additions. The final report on this study was expected to be received by Applicant late in September or early in October (1976).
Another important determinant of the economic justifiability of peak load pricing for any given system is the shape of its load curve. There are much greater benefits from peak load pricing potentially available to a system having sharp peaks and deep valleys in its load curve than to one having a relatively flat curve. These relationships may be expressed in terms of load factor (ratio of average annual system demand to annual peak demand). In 1975 the maximum monthly load factor for the Duke Power System reached a value of about 76.7 percent and is approximately 70 percent during 8 months of the year. In addition, monthly minimum loads on the system varied from 29 to 36 percent of annual peak load. This suggests that, although there is a limit to the effectiveness of flattening load curves, the load characteristics of the Duke Power Company are such that there may be some opportunity for load flattening.
